8e37ec89a058e3a46c1b9d2a72834771630f2827.summary: F-Secure announced in July 2013 a Mac OS X trojan, Janicab, disguised as a PDF. It uses a right-to-left override character so the name hides a .app extension, and it is code-signed, so Mac OS X runs it after one approval. It installs components in a hidden folder in the home directory, creates a cron job, contacts a command server, and takes screenshots and records audio. Most antivirus software did not detect it at the time. A later update says the developer certificate was revoked. The post gives removal steps and warns users to back up first.

dates.what: Report published; F-Secure announced the trojan's discovery.

dates.q: July 16, 2013: Looks like the developer certificate used to sign this trojan has already been revoked.
dates.what: Update: the developer certificate used to sign the trojan was reported revoked.

techniques.v: disguising an application as a document
techniques.q: disguising an application as a document to trick the user into opening it
is that the app is signed. Thus, the system will allow it to run unimpeded, as long as you approve it on the first run.
When run, the trojan opens a document to avoid causing further suspicion.
the app installs a number of components in an invisible folder
creates a cron job to keep components running
locates its command & control server by searching a few specific places for specific text that contains an IP address.
it begins taking screenshots and recording audio,

techniques.q: At this time, Janicab is not detected by most anti-virus software

hedges: The author presumes the malware uses cron because it is older technology, which is an inference rather than a confirmed finding.
The author does not yet know which Mac OS X versions the malware can infect.
Detection status is stated only for the time of writing: 'At this time, Janicab is not detected by most anti-virus software.'
The account of the hidden folder and cron job is relayed from F-Secure's post, not verified by the author.
The author says seeing a signed app used by malware 'may indicate' that Gatekeeper offers less security than hoped.
The later revocation update is tentative: 'Looks like the developer certificate ... has already been revoked.'
